paragraphs: Governments Is Increasing, Although the Persons Who Govern Are Less Stable

Looking back over what has been said so far, the reader will be startled and alarmed to find that in Europe everything seems to work toward an unlimited extension of the government’s prerogatives. It seems also to make everyone who enjoyed the rights of private independence weaker, more dependent, and more insecure. The democratic nations of Europe have all the general and lasting tendencies that push the Americans toward the centralization of government. On top of that, they are exposed to a number of secondary and accidental causes that the Americans do not know. It seems as though every step they take toward equality brings them closer to despotism. And in fact, if we simply look around us, we shall be convinced that this is so. In the aristocratic ages before our own, the sovereigns of Europe had been stripped of many of the rights that belong to their power, or had given them up. Less than a hundred years ago, in most European nations, numerous private persons and corporations were independent enough to administer justice, to raise and maintain troops, to levy taxes, and often even to make or interpret the law. The state has taken back for itself alone these natural attributes of sovereign power everywhere. In every matter of government it tolerates no intermediary between itself and the people, and in general business it directs the people by its own direct influence. I am far from blaming this concentration of power. I only point it out.

In the same period Europe had a great number of secondary powers, which represented local interests and administered local affairs. Most of these local authorities have already disappeared, and all are rapidly tending either to disappear or to fall into complete dependence. From one end of Europe to the other, the privileges of the nobility, the liberties of cities, and the powers of provincial bodies are either destroyed or close to destruction. In the last half-century Europe has lived through many revolutions and counter-revolutions, which have driven it in opposite directions. But all these upheavals resemble one another in one respect: they have all shaken or destroyed the secondary powers of government. The local privileges that the French did not abolish in the countries they conquered have finally given way to the policy of the princes who conquered the French. Those princes rejected every innovation of the French Revolution except centralization. That is the only principle they agreed to accept from such a source. My point is that all these various rights, wrested in our time one after another from classes, corporations, and individuals, have not been used to build new secondary powers on a more democratic basis. They have uniformly been concentrated in the sovereign’s hands. Everywhere the state gains more and more direct control over the humblest members of the community, and a more exclusive power to govern each of them in his smallest concerns. *a Almost all the charitable establishments of Europe used to be in the hands of private persons or corporations. Now they depend almost entirely on the supreme government, and in many countries that power actually runs them. The state takes on almost exclusively the task of giving bread to the hungry, help and shelter to the sick, and work to the idle, and it acts as the sole reliever of every kind of misery. Education, like charity, has become in most countries today a national concern. The state receives the child from its mother’s arms, and often takes it, in order to hand it over to official agents. The state undertakes to train the heart and instruct the mind of each generation. Public instruction follows a uniform course, as everything else does, and diversity, like freedom, is vanishing day by day. Nor do I hesitate to affirm that among almost all the Christian nations of our day, Catholic as well as Protestant, religion is in danger of falling into the hands of the government. It is not that rulers are overly jealous of the right to settle points of doctrine. But they take a firmer and firmer hold on the will of those who expound doctrine. They deprive the clergy of their property and pay them salaries. They divert the influence of the priesthood to their own use and make priests their own ministers, often their own servants. Through this alliance with religion they reach the inner depths of the human soul. *b

[Footnote a: This gradual weakening of individuals in relation to society as a whole can be traced in a thousand ways. From among these examples I shall choose one drawn from the law of wills. In aristocracies it is common to profess the deepest reverence for a man’s last testamentary wishes. Among the older nations of Europe this feeling sometimes even became superstitious. The power of the state, far from interfering with the whims of a dying man, gave full force to the smallest of them and secured for him a perpetual power. When all living men are enfeebled, the will of the dead gets less respect. It is confined within a narrow range, and beyond that range the supreme power of the laws annuls or checks it. In the Middle Ages, testamentary power had, so to speak, no limits. Among the French today, a man cannot divide his fortune among his children without the state’s interference. Having domineered over a whole life, the law insists on regulating the very last act of it.]

[Footnote b: As the duties of the central power grow, the number of public officials who represent that power must grow too. They form a nation within each nation, and since they share the government’s stability, they increasingly fill the place of an aristocracy.
In almost every part of Europe the government rules in two ways. It rules one part of the community through their fear of its agents, and the other part through their hope of becoming its agents.]

But this is still only one side of the picture. As we have just seen, the authority of government has spread throughout the sphere of all existing powers until that sphere can no longer hold it. It goes further and invades the domain that used to be reserved to private independence. In our time a multitude of actions that were formerly entirely beyond the control of the public administration have been placed under it, and their number keeps growing. Among aristocratic nations the supreme government usually contented itself with managing and supervising the community in whatever directly and visibly touched the national honor. In all other respects the people were left to follow their own free will. Among these nations the government often seemed to forget that there is a point at which the faults and sufferings of private persons affect the general prosperity, and that preventing the ruin of a private individual must sometimes be a matter of public importance. The democratic nations of our time lean toward the opposite extreme. It is evident that most of our rulers will not be content with governing the people collectively. They seem to think themselves responsible for the actions and private condition of their subjects. They seem to have undertaken to guide and instruct each of them through the various events of life, and to secure their happiness quite apart from their own consent. Private individuals, for their part, are more and more inclined to see the supreme power in the same light. They call on its help in all their needs, and they look to the administration as their mentor and guide.

I assert that in no country of Europe has the public administration failed to become not only more centralized but also more inquisitive and more minute. Everywhere it meddles in private concerns more than it did. It regulates more undertakings, and smaller ones, and every day it gains a firmer footing around, above, and about all private persons, to assist, advise, and coerce them. A sovereign used to live on the income of his lands or the revenue from his taxes. That is no longer so, now that his wants have grown along with his power. In circumstances that once forced a prince to impose a new tax, he now turns to a loan. Thus the state gradually becomes the debtor of most of the wealthier members of the community and centralizes the largest amounts of capital in its own hands. It draws small capital into its keeping by another method. As men mingle and conditions become more equal, the poor have more resources, more education, and more desires. They form the idea of improving their condition, and this teaches them to save. Their savings are daily producing an endless number of small capitals, the slow and gradual yield of labor, and these keep growing. But most of this money would be unproductive if it stayed scattered in its owners’ hands. This fact has given rise to a philanthropic institution that, unless I am mistaken, will soon become one of our most important political institutions. Some charitable persons conceived the idea of collecting the savings of the poor and putting them out at interest. In some countries these benevolent associations are still entirely separate from the state. But in almost all of them they clearly tend to merge with the government, and in some the government has replaced them. It has taken on the enormous task of gathering in one place, and lending out at interest on its own responsibility, the daily savings of many millions of working people. Thus the state draws the wealth of the rich to itself by loans, and it has the poor man’s mite at its disposal in the savings banks. The wealth of the country is perpetually flowing around the government and passing through its hands. The accumulation grows in step with the equality of conditions, because in a democratic country the state alone inspires confidence in private individuals, since it alone seems to have strength and permanence. *c So the sovereign does not limit himself to managing the public treasury. He interferes in private money matters. He is the superior, and often the master, of all the members of the community, and on top of that he takes the role of their steward and paymaster.

[Footnote c: Two things are happening at once. The appetite for worldly comfort never stops growing, and the government keeps gaining fuller control of the sources of that comfort. So men are heading toward servitude along two separate roads. Their appetite for their own well-being keeps them from taking part in government, and their love of that well-being makes them ever more dependent on those who govern.]

The central power not only performs by itself all the duties once discharged by various authorities, extending those duties and surpassing those authorities. It also performs them with more alertness, strength, and independence than it showed before. In our time all the governments of Europe have remarkably improved the science of administration. They do more things, and they do everything with more order, more speed, and less expense. They seem to be constantly enriched by all the experience they have taken from private persons. From day to day the princes of Europe hold their subordinate officers under stricter control, and they invent new methods for guiding them more closely and inspecting them with less trouble. They are not content to manage everything through their agents. They undertake to manage their agents’ conduct in everything. So the public administration not only depends on one and the same power, but is also more and more confined to one spot and concentrated in the same hands. The government centralizes its agency while it increases its prerogative, and the result is a twofold increase of strength.

When we examine the ancient constitution of the judicial power among most European nations, two things strike us: the independence of that power and the extent of its functions. Not only did the courts of justice decide almost all disputes between private persons, but in very many cases they acted as arbiters between private persons and the state. I am not speaking here of the political and administrative offices that courts had seized in some countries, but of the judicial office that all of them shared. In most countries of Europe there were, and there still are, many private rights, linked for the most part to the general right of property, that stood under the protection of the courts of justice. The state could not violate them without the courts’ sanction. This semi-political power was what chiefly distinguished the European courts from all others. All nations have had judges, but not all have given their judges the same privileges. Look at what is happening now among the democratic nations of Europe that are called free, and among the others as well. New and more dependent courts are springing up everywhere beside the old ones, for the express purpose of deciding, by an extraordinary jurisdiction, any disputed matters that may arise between the government and private persons. The older judicial power keeps its independence, but its jurisdiction is narrowed, and there is a growing tendency to reduce it to serving only as the arbiter between private interests. The number of these special courts keeps increasing, and so do their functions. Thus the government is more and more freed from the need to submit its policy and its rights to the sanction of another power. Judges cannot be done without, but at least the state chooses them and always holds them under its control. So between the government and private individuals they put the image of justice rather than justice itself. The state is not satisfied with drawing all affairs to itself. It acquires an ever-growing power to decide on all of them without restriction and without appeal. *d

[Footnote d: A strange sophism has been advanced on this subject in France. When a suit arises between the government and a private person, it is not to be tried before an ordinary judge, in order, they say, not to mix the administrative and judicial powers. As if giving the government the office of judging and administering at the same time were not mixing those powers, and mixing them in the most dangerous and oppressive way.]

Among the modern nations of Europe there is one great cause, separate from all those already pointed out, that perpetually helps to extend the agency of the supreme power or to strengthen its prerogative, though it has not received enough attention. I mean the growth of manufactures, which the progress of social equality fosters. Manufactures generally gather a multitude of men in one place, and new and complicated relations spring up among them. By their trade these men are exposed to sharp and sudden swings between plenty and want, and public tranquility is endangered during them. It may also happen that these occupations sacrifice the health, and even the life, of those who profit from them or who live by them. So the manufacturing classes need more regulation, supervision, and restraint than the other classes of society, and it is natural that the powers of government should grow in the same proportion as those classes.

This is a truth of general application. What follows concerns the nations of Europe in particular. In the centuries before our own, the aristocracy owned the soil and was able to defend it. Landed property was therefore surrounded by ample safeguards, and its owners enjoyed great independence. This gave rise to laws and customs that have lasted despite the division of land and the ruin of the nobility. Even now, landowners and farmers are still the members of the community who most easily escape the control of the supreme power. In those same aristocratic ages, to which all the sources of our history go back, personal property was of small importance, and those who held it were despised and weak. The manufacturing class was an exception within those aristocratic communities. It had no sure patronage, it was not protected from outside, and it was often unable to protect itself.

Hence a habit grew up of regarding manufacturing property as something of a particular nature. It was not owed the same deference or worth the same safeguards as property in general, and manufacturers were seen as a small class within the mass of the people, whose independence mattered little and who could properly be abandoned to the disciplinary passions of princes. When we glance through the codes of the Middle Ages, we are surprised to see how many royal regulations hampered manufactures, down to their smallest details, in those periods of personal independence. On this point centralization was as active and as minute as it can ever be. Since then a great revolution has taken place in the world. Manufacturing property, then only in embryo, has spread until it covers Europe. The manufacturing class has grown in numbers and wealth from the remnants of all other ranks. It has kept growing, and it is still growing in number, in importance, and in wealth. Almost everyone who does not belong to it is tied to it at some point at least. After having been an exception in society, it threatens to become the chief class, if not the only one. Nevertheless, the ideas and political precedents it produced long ago still cling to it. These ideas and precedents stay unchanged, because they are old, and also because they happen to fit perfectly with the new ideas and general habits of our contemporaries. Manufacturing property, then, does not extend its rights in proportion to its importance. The manufacturing classes do not become less dependent as they become more numerous. On the contrary, it seems as though despotism lurked within them and naturally grew with their growth. *e As a nation becomes more engaged in manufactures, it feels more strongly the lack of roads, canals, harbors, and other works of a semi-public nature that make it easier to acquire wealth. And as a nation becomes more democratic, private individuals become less able, and the state more able, to carry out works on such a scale. I do not hesitate to assert that the clear tendency of all governments at present is to take on the execution of these undertakings entirely by themselves, and by doing so they hold the population they govern in closer dependence every day.

[Footnote e: I shall cite a few facts in support of this remark. Mines are the natural sources of manufacturing wealth. As manufactures have grown up in Europe, the output of mines has become of more general importance, and good mining has become harder because of the division of property, which is a consequence of the equality of conditions. Most governments have claimed a right to own the soil in which the mines lie and to inspect the workings, which has never been done with any other kind of property. Thus mines, which were private property, subject to the same obligations and sheltered by the same guarantees as all other landed property, have fallen under the control of the state. The state either works them or leases them. Their owners are mere tenants, deriving their rights from the state. Moreover, the state almost everywhere claims the power to direct their operations. It lays down rules, requires particular methods to be adopted, and subjects the mining adventurers to constant supervision. If they resist, a government court of justice removes them, and the government transfers their contract to other hands. So the government not only owns the mines but has all the adventurers in its power. Nevertheless, as manufactures increase, the working of old mines increases too. New ones are opened, and the mining population spreads and grows. Day by day governments enlarge their underground dominions and populate them with their agents.]

On the other hand, as the power of a state grows and its needs increase, the state’s own consumption of manufactured goods keeps growing larger, and these goods are generally made in the arsenals or establishments of the government. Thus in every kingdom the ruler becomes the principal manufacturer. He gathers and keeps in his service a vast number of engineers, architects, mechanics, and craftsmen. Not only is he the principal manufacturer, but he tends more and more to become the chief of all the other manufacturers, or rather their master. Private persons grow more powerless as they grow more equal, so they can accomplish nothing in manufactures without combination. The government, naturally, seeks to bring these combinations under its own control.

It must be admitted that these collective beings, called combinations, are stronger and more formidable than a private individual can ever be, and that they bear less responsibility for their own actions. From this it seems reasonable that they should not be allowed to keep so much independence from the supreme government as might be granted to a private individual.

Rulers are all the more inclined to follow this policy because their own inclinations invite them to it. Among democratic nations the people’s resistance to the government can show itself only through association. So the government always looks with disfavor on associations that are not in its own power. It is also well worth noticing that among democratic nations the people themselves often feel a secret fear and jealousy toward these very associations, which keeps the citizens from defending institutions they need so much. The power and the longevity of these small private bodies, amid the weakness and instability of the whole community, astonish and alarm the people. The free use that each association makes of its natural powers is almost regarded as a dangerous privilege. Moreover, all the associations that spring up in our age are new corporate powers whose rights time has not sanctioned. They come into existence when the idea of private rights is weak and the power of government is unbounded, so it is no wonder that they lose their freedom at birth. Among all European nations there are some kinds of associations that cannot be formed until the state has examined their bylaws and authorized their existence. In several others, attempts are made to extend this rule to all associations. The consequences of such a policy, if it succeeded, are easy to foresee. Once the sovereign had a general right to authorize associations of every kind on certain conditions, he would soon claim the right to supervise and manage them, so as to keep them from departing from the rules he had laid down. In this way the state, having made all who wish to form associations dependent on it, would go on to reduce to the same condition everyone who belongs to associations already formed, that is to say, almost all the men now living. Governments thus take over, and turn to their own purposes, most of the new power that manufacturing interests have brought into the world in our time. Manufacturers govern us; they govern manufactures.

I attach so much importance to all that I have just said that I am tormented by the fear of having weakened my meaning in trying to make it clearer. Suppose the reader thinks the examples I have offered to support my observations are insufficient or badly chosen. Suppose he imagines that I have somewhere exaggerated the encroachments of the supreme power, and on the other hand that I have underestimated the sphere still open to the exertions of individual independence. I beg him to put the book down for a moment and to think for himself about the subjects I have tried to explain. Let him look closely at what is happening in France and in other countries. Let him ask those around him. Let him search himself. I am much mistaken if he does not arrive, without my guidance and by other paths, at the point to which I have tried to lead him. He will see that for the last half-century centralization has been growing everywhere in a thousand different ways. Wars, revolutions, and conquests have promoted it, and all men have worked to increase it. During the same period men have followed one another at the head of affairs with remarkable speed, and their ideas, interests, and passions have been endlessly varied. Yet all of them have, by one means or another, sought to centralize. This instinctive centralization has been the one fixed point amid the extreme changeability of their lives and thoughts.

Suppose the reader, having studied these details of human affairs, tries to take in the whole broad prospect. He will be struck by the result. On one side he will see the most settled dynasties shaken or overthrown. Peoples everywhere are violently escaping the rule of their laws and abolishing or limiting the authority of their rulers or princes. The nations that are not in open revolution are at least restless and excited, and all of them are animated by the same spirit of revolt. On the other side, in this very period of anarchy and among these unruly nations, the prerogative of the supreme government is growing without pause. It becomes more centralized, more adventurous, more absolute, and more extensive. The people fall continually under the control of the public administration. They are led, without noticing it, to give up to it some further portion of their individual independence, until the very men who from time to time overturn a throne and trample on a line of kings bow more and more servilely to the slightest dictate of a clerk. Thus two contrary revolutions seem to be under way in our day. One continually weakens the supreme power, and the other continually strengthens it. At no other time in our history has that power seemed so weak or so strong. But if we look more attentively at the state of the world, it appears that these two revolutions are closely connected, that they spring from the same source, and that after following separate courses they lead men at last to the same result. I may venture to repeat once more what I have already said or implied in several parts of this book. We must take great care not to confuse the principle of equality itself with the revolution that finally establishes that principle in a nation’s social condition and laws. Here lies the reason for almost all the phenomena that astonish us. All the old political powers of Europe, the greatest as well as the least, were founded in ages of aristocracy, and they more or less represented or defended the principles of inequality and privilege. To make the new wants and interests that the growing principle of equality brought in prevail in government, our contemporaries had to overturn or coerce the established powers. This led them to make revolutions, and it breathed into many of them that fierce love of disturbance and independence which all revolutions, whatever their object, always produce. I do not believe there is a single country in Europe where the progress of equality has not been preceded or followed by some violent changes in the state of property and persons. Almost all these changes have come with much anarchy and license, because they were made by the least civilized part of the nation against the most civilized. From this came the two contrary tendencies I have just pointed out. While the democratic revolution was glowing with heat, the men bent on destroying the old aristocratic powers that opposed it showed a strong spirit of independence. But as the victory of the principle of equality became more complete, they gradually surrendered to the propensities natural to that condition of equality, and they strengthened and centralized their governments. They had sought to be free in order to make themselves equal. But the more equality was established with the help of freedom, the harder freedom itself became to attain.

These two conditions of a nation have sometimes existed together. The last generation in France showed how a people could build a monstrous tyranny within the community at the very time they were thwarting the authority of the nobility and defying the power of all kings. They taught the world at once how to win freedom and how to lose it. In our day men see established powers falling apart on every side. They see all ancient authority gasping its last and all ancient barriers tottering toward their fall, and the judgment of the wisest is troubled by the sight. They attend only to the astonishing revolution taking place before their eyes, and they imagine that mankind is about to fall into perpetual anarchy. If they looked to the final consequences of this revolution, their fears might perhaps take a different shape. For my part, I confess that I put no trust in the spirit of freedom that seems to animate my contemporaries. I can see well enough that the nations of this age are turbulent, but I do not clearly see that they are liberal. And I fear that, when the disturbances that rock the foundations of thrones have ended, the domination of sovereigns may prove more powerful than it ever was before.
